Computation and Language.summary: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love trains", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, perform far worse. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.
Computation and Language.comment: Code available at https://github.com/OzAmram/psm-mixture-test; v2 fixes an issue with classifier baselines, main results unchanged

Computation and Language.title: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment
Computation and Language.summary: Emergent misalignment (EM) has been linked to the activation of misaligned persona vectors and evil character traits, suggesting that EM operates through disruption of the model's aligned character rather than direct learning of harmful content. Motivated by this connection, we study self-modeling interventions: specifically self-recognition and self-reports as character-targeted interventions that are distinct from existing in-training defenses. We conduct two-stage finetuning experiments across three models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct) and multiple EM datasets to compare self-recognition finetuning against benign finetuning baselines (correct domain-specific data, general knowledge, and word counting), finding it an effective defense in both reversal and prevention settings. For prevention, only self-recognition finetuning consistently reduces misalignment without exacerbating any individual metric, suggesting that character fortification specifically drives prevention. We also conduct in-training experiments across these models to compare the effectiveness of self-reports with benign interleaving and inoculation prompting. We provide further evidence for EM's relation to the LLM's default character by showing that EM finetuning leads to fragmentation of LLM's identity self-reports, reduces self-recognition performance to about chance, artificially corrupting self-recognition exacerbates misalignment caused by EM finetuning, and finetuning on self-reports from EM finetuned models can transfer misalignment. Together, these findings reframe EM not as the adoption of a coherent misaligned persona but as the destabilization of aligned character.

Computation and Language.title: Do Reasoning LLMs Refuse What They Infer in Long Contexts?
Computation and Language.summary: Long-context LLMs can infer objectives that are not explicitly stated. This capability is useful for reasoning over documents, code, and tool traces, but it also introduces a safety risk. Harmful intent can be distributed across a context and become apparent only after the model combines the relevant information. Existing safety evaluations largely focus on explicitly stated harmful requests and therefore do not fully capture this failure mode. We introduce compositional reasoning attacks, a long-context attack setting in which harmful requests are decomposed into semantically incomplete fragments and embedded in long contexts. The final query is neutral, and the model must retrieve and combine the fragments to infer the implied harmful objective. Empirically, we show that models generally refuse harmful requests when they are explicitly stated. However, refusal rates drop when the same objectives must be reconstructed from fragments, and these failures often become more pronounced in longer contexts. Our analyses suggest that this gap cannot be explained by retrieval difficulties alone. Models can often reconstruct the harmful objective but do not reliably refuse it. Increasing inference-time reasoning effort improves refusal, but at a higher computational cost, with unsafe responses still occurring. Our results reveal a long-context safety gap: Models are better at refusing harmful requests they see than harmful objectives they infer.

Computation and Language.title: Decode Token Parallelism: Memory-Efficient Distributed Attention Parallelism for Scalable LLM Decoding
Computation and Language.summary: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts requires KV-cache capacity and attention bandwidth that grow with the decode pool. Existing parallelization strategies trade one against the other: data parallelism replicates model weights, limiting KV capacity; tensor parallelism stops scaling attention at the model's KV-head count and pushes dense collectives across nodes; and decode context parallelism (DCP) recovers capacity by sharding the sequence but adds cross-node aggregation of partial attention results. We observe that during decode, dense layers and attention scale differently: dense layers amortize weight reads across the batch and run efficiently within a single NVLink domain, whereas attention cost grows with every active request's KV cache. We present Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP), a decode-pool architecture that decouples weight placement from attention ownership. TKNP distributes a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks. The active node holding a block executes its projections and MLP for the full batch using intra-node tensor parallelism, while every node computes attention for its own requests against locally resident KV cache. This extends request-local attention across nodes without replicating weights: only current-token activations cross the network, dense all-reduces remain within NVLink, and attention requires no cross-node merging of partial results. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B on up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP improves completion throughput for long-context, high-concurrency workloads by up to 1.7$\times$ over DCP and by up to 2.06$\times$ over data parallelism at matched GPU count.

Computation and Language.title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
Computation and Language.summary: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

Computation and Language.title: Semantic Motion Anchors: Bridging Motion and Meaning in Co-Speech Gestures
Computation and Language.summary: Learning a shared representation between spoken text and gesture is central to co-speech gesture retrieval, synthesis, and understanding, but remains challenging for semantically meaningful gestures whose communicative intent is not captured by motion alone. Direct contrastive alignment between transcripts and continuous motion embeddings often overemphasizes low-level kinematics and misses the symbolic content of semantic gestures. We propose semantic motion anchors, natural-language abstractions of gesture motion capturing physical form and communicative intent. Our method discretizes 3D gestures into body-hand motion primitives, verbalizes them into structured descriptions, and grounds them in the transcript to provide auxiliary contrastive supervision. On BEAT2, our method improves text-to-gesture R@1 by 8.2% over a direct text-motion baseline and outperforms prior retrieval approaches on text to gesture and gesture to text retrieval directions. Beyond aggregate retrieval metrics, semantic motion anchor supervision helps retrieve gestures that are semantically meaningful for the spoken query, rather than defaulting to generic motion patterns. A downstream retrieval-augmented gesture generation study showed that users significantly preferred gestures retrieved by our approach over a retrieval-augmented generation baseline, demonstrating that semantically grounded retrieval translates to gestures that better convey communicative intent in downstream generation.

Computation and Language.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
Computation and Language.summary: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
Computation and Language.comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, 5 appendices. To appear at NeurIPS 2026

Computation and Language.title: Domain-Routed Delta Optimization for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Computation and Language.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation assigns each sample a domain teacher but typically updates shared student parameters. We introduce Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (DRD-MOPD), which specifies which parameter components each domain's samples update. The student is the sum of a frozen base and trainable components initialized from expert-minus-base weights. All components participate in every forward pass; four update modes define the correspondence between sample domains and components, each with independent optimizer states. We analyze these update rules and measure retention of the original expert geometry through angles, projection coefficients, and energy. Prior work such as Open-MOPD distills directly from the base model; 97.02% of its released final checkpoint's increment energy lies outside the span of the original expert directions. In comparison, our Own checkpoint after 20 updates retains coefficients near one along each component's original direction and pairwise angles ranging from 88.04 to 92.41 degrees; its exported BF16 student's increment has 4.90% outside energy, versus 10.52% for the sum of saved FP32 components. The same checkpoint achieves a 32.72% macro score across six benchmarks, compared with 32.44% for its initial task-arithmetic merge. These measurements describe geometry and capability at the evaluated training stages and settings.

Computation and Language.title: From Architecture to Output: Testing the Structural Origins of Hallucination and the Amplifying Role of Data
Computation and Language.summary: Surveys of hallucination classify errors by how an output relates to its source, and often explain them by the model's structure: attention retrieves by association, the maximum-likelihood objective has no term for truth, and left-to-right decoding commits to early tokens. Data, on this account, makes these failures worse rather than causing them. The account is usually argued rather than tested. We test it with interventions that need only sampling access. Study 1 holds pretraining data, tokenizer and scale fixed and swaps attention for a state-space mixer, using five Pythia/Mamba pairs from 130M to 2.8B parameters and four further attention models, on 111 facts presented with a planted false or a planted true statement. Swapping the mixer leaves free-recall failure unchanged (both 2.8B models answer 3 of 200 SimpleQA questions), but it changes what happens to a defect in the input. From 410M upwards, every attention model repeats the planted falsehood more often than its matched state-space model (2.8B: 650 vs. 566 of 666 items, p = 2.5e-20), also on facts both models know, while the state-space models can still read planted facts they did not know. Study 2 replaces the first wrong fact in 111 erroneous answers from three instruction-tuned models. The correct fact cuts the share of answers with a downstream error from 92.5% to 48.1%, but a different wrong fact works as well (p = 0.38), and the models give the right answer in isolation on only 2 of 111 items. The structural account survives in a narrower form. The mixing component decides whether a defect in the context becomes an output error, commitment decides how an error spreads, and on long-tail questions the first error comes from missing knowledge, not from a suppressed truth.
Computation and Language.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Substantially revised: adds a matched-architecture study (14 models) and corrected statistics for the prefix-repair study. Data and code in ancillary files

Computation and Language.title: Characterising divergence between heuristic and language-model ratings of mobile user interface quality
Computation and Language.summary: Automated assessment of mobile user interface quality is attractive because manual review does not scale, and large language models are increasingly proposed for the task. Whether their ratings correspond to those produced by established rule-based heuristics has not been characterised at scale. We construct a 15,000-screen corpus from the RICO dataset using six documented filters, score every screen with a literature-grounded heuristic scorer, and collect ratings from three open-weight language models across two input representations, yielding 270,000 ratings. We report linearly weighted Cohen's kappa with bootstrap confidence intervals, offset-corrected kappa, intraclass correlation, and Bland-Altman limits of agreement, together with a chance baseline for the tolerance-band agreement rule. Agreement between the two rating sources is consistently weak: raw kappa falls below 0.15 in seventeen of eighteen model-representation-dimension cells. However, fifteen of eighteen cells are statistically distinguishable from zero, and correcting for a constant offset raises five cells above 0.15, so the divergence is better described as a combination of systematic bias and weak covariation than as absence of relationship. Model ratings track structural properties of the interface, but substantially less strongly than the heuristic does, and more strongly from an untruncated structural element list than from a screenshot. We further show that dimensions elicited in a single generated response are correlated by construction, reaching rho = 0.97 in one condition, which constrains what such designs can measure. We report these results as a characterisation of divergence between two automated raters rather than as evidence that either is correct, and we set out the validation a stronger claim would require.
Computation and Language.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables (incl. appendix). Data and code in ancillary files. An earlier abstract was presented at EFAST 2026 under the title "Seeing Without Understanding: Large Language Model Evaluation of Mobile User Interface Quality, Failure Taxonomy, and Architectural Explanation"

Computation and Language.title: Hidden Measurement Error in LLM Pipelines Distorts Annotation, Evaluation, and Benchmarking
Computation and Language.summary: LLM evaluations drive model deployment, safety standards, research conclusions, and future projections, for example, about AI's impact on the labor market. Yet the way we often estimate noise from autoraters (LLM-as-judge) ignores variability from factors like judge model choice and prompt phrasing, which means we're underestimating error in a way that worsens with more data. This unmeasured variance can affect results enough to reverse conclusions. And judge-pipelines that fail to average this variation are more vulnerable to "benchmark hacking". This paper introduces a framework we call "total evaluation error (TEE)," which decomposes LLM pipeline uncertainty and uses design-study projections to reduce total error. In our safety and ideology applications, naive standard errors are 53-70% smaller than the corrected SE under our TEE framework. Using Chatbot Arena data, we show naive 95% CI coverage drops as n grows, while TEE-corrected coverage holds at 95%, and TEE-guided pipelines restrict the potential range of benchmark gaming by roughly 43%. We show further that a small pilot allows for the estimation of proper CIs, with the added benefit of projecting which design changes most improve precision. Using those projections to allocate API calls cut MMLU estimation error roughly in half against the answer key at the same budget, and increased per-match agreement with human voters on Chatbot Arena by 7.9 percentage points.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 14 pages, 7 figures. SI Appendix: https://solomonmg.github.io/pdf/totalevalerror_si.pdf

Computation and Language.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement across Seven Open Reasoning Models
Computation and Language.summary: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Across 94k ShareGPT conversations, 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and the task cost of this stripping remains unmeasured. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, 794 tasks, and the official checker. The same deletion spans -4.4 to +51.3 points with both ends excluding zero, and for the one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property. The reading follows the model itself and stays constant across deployments, and a retrained or re-released model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing and aggregation as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

Computation and Language.title: Understanding and Tackling Label Errors in Individual-Level Nature Language Understanding
Computation and Language.summary: Natural language understanding (NLU) is a task that enables machines to understand human language. Some tasks, such as stance detection and sentiment analysis, are closely related to individual subjective perspectives, thus termed individual-level NLU. Previously, these tasks are often simplified to text-level NLU tasks, ignoring individual factors. This not only makes inference difficult and unexplainable but often results in a large number of label errors when creating datasets. To address the above limitations, we propose a new NLU annotation guideline based on individual-level factors. Specifically, we incorporate other posts by the same individual and then annotate individual subjective perspectives after considering all individual posts. We use this guideline to expand and re-annotate the stance detection and topic-based sentiment analysis datasets. We find that error rates in the samples were as high as 31.7\% and 23.3\%. We further use large language models to conduct experiments on the re-annotation datasets and find that the large language models perform well on both datasets after adding individual factors. Both GPT-4o and Llama3-70B can achieve an accuracy greater than 87\% on the re-annotation datasets. We also verify the effectiveness of individual factors through ablation studies. We call on future researchers to add individual factors when creating such datasets. Our re-annotation dataset can be found at https://github.com/24yearsoldstudent/Individual-NLU
Computation and Language.comment: Best Paper Award in International Conference on Advances in Social Network Analysis and Mining (ASONAM) 2026

Information Retrieval.title: High-dimensional Regret Minimization
Information Retrieval.summary:
Multi-criteria decision making over large databases is fundamental to many real-world applications. Interactive regret minimization has emerged recently as a promising approach that combines the controllable output size of top-$k$ queries with the flexibility of skyline queries, without requiring users to explicitly specify a utility function. Instead, the system iteratively presents a small set of options, learns the user's implicit preferences from their selections, and progressively refines its recommendations.
  However, modern applications such as housing search and financial product selection often involve hundreds of attributes. Existing interactive methods either fail to scale to such high-dimensional data or require excessive user interaction, frequently exceeding $1000$ rounds. We address this limitation with FHDR (Fast High-Dimensional Reduction), a framework that exploits sparse linear preferences to discover key attributes through lightweight interactions. We also propose AttributeSubset, an efficient single-round algorithm that returns a compact recommendation set without further feedback. In our experiments on real datasets, FHDR completes in under $0.03$s and requires fewer than $30$ interaction rounds under the default setting.
  Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that FHDR outperforms the best-known baselines by at least one order of magnitude in execution time and by up to several orders of magnitude in interaction cost. These results establish FHDR as a new state of the art for scalable interactive regret minimization.

Information Retrieval.title: JUÁ -- A Benchmark for Information Retrieval in Brazilian Legal Text Collections
Information Retrieval.summary: Legal information retrieval in Portuguese remains difficult to evaluate systematically because available datasets differ widely in document type, query style, and relevance definition. We present JUÁ, a public benchmark for Brazilian legal retrieval designed to support more reproducible and comparable evaluation across heterogeneous legal collections. More broadly, JUÁ is intended not only as a benchmark, but as a continuous evaluation infrastructure for Brazilian legal IR, combining shared protocols, common ranking metrics, fixed splits when applicable, and a public leaderboard. The benchmark covers jurisprudence retrieval as well as broader legislative, regulatory, and question-driven legal search. We evaluate lexical, dense, and BM25-based reranking pipelines, including a domain-adapted Qwen embedding model fine-tuned on JUÁ-aligned supervision. Results show that the benchmark is sufficiently heterogeneous to distinguish retrieval paradigms and reveal substantial cross-dataset trade-offs. Domain adaptation yields its clearest gains on the supervision-aligned JUÁ-Juris subset, while BM25 remains highly competitive on other collections, especially in settings with strong lexical and institutional phrasing cues. Overall, JUÁ provides a practical evaluation framework for studying legal retrieval across multiple Brazilian legal domains under a common benchmark design.

Information Retrieval.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
Information Retrieval.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

Information Retrieval.title: NIFT-SQL: Customer-Supervised Table Scoring for Enterprise Text-to-SQL Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Enterprise text-to-SQL starts with finding the tables a question needs, which is hard when a schema spans several databases and hundreds of cryptic tables. We ask whether models trained separately on each customer's example questions, reading only table names, column names, and declared keys, improve table retrieval. NIFT-SQL (Necessity-Informed Fusion for Text-to-SQL) fuses hybrid search over a retriever fine-tuned on the customer's questions with a fine-tuned 560M cross-encoder that scores every table for whether the query needs it, through a logistic regression fitted on held-out questions. On BEAVER, LiveSQLBench, and LiveSQLBench-Large (244 to 971 tables; four splits, three trainings), NIFT-SQL places every reference table in the top 15 for 69.2%, 89.5%, and 85.6% of test questions, against 30.4%, 41.0%, and 21.8% for hybrid search and 61.1%, 81.7%, and 70.4% for the fine-tuned retriever with the same labels. With off-the-shelf search, the cross-encoder without fine-tuning is 21 points lower. A zero-shot 8B reranker needs no labels and, routed by database, shows no resolved complete@15 difference on two collections; adding its scores as two fusion features gives a high-accuracy mode that reaches 72.4%, 92.5%, and 88.6%, ahead of the validation-selected zero-shot reranker variant on two collections, with no resolved difference on the third. Rank fusion of the two trained parts, grouped by database, shows no resolved difference from the learned fusion. Scored once on a newer BEAVER release, NIFT-SQL beats search and leads the label-matched retriever at top 8 on the synthetic test, but trails it at top 15 on real questions.

Information Retrieval.title: Scaling Taxonomy-Free Image Labeling with Generative AI: A Multimodal
Information Retrieval.summary:
Providing real-time multimodal insights into images is challenging because it requires low latency, high description accuracy, and scalable solutions that are both cost-effective and efficient. For example, given a new image of an outfit, we would like to generate insights that the image depicts "earth tones" and "linen pants" and allow users to explore similar ideas along these themes. Traditional strategies to generate such insights would typically involve building taxonomies producing a golden set labeled by humans, training models on these datasets, and deploying these models for online inference services. Such workflows are constrained by fixed taxonomy, high labeling cost, limited labeling coverage in sample space, and human errors and expertise gaps in labelers. In addition, these methods are expensive and cumbersome to iterate over time. Recent trends have started exploring generative AI models for online insights, but this method suffers from long latency and prohibitive costs to support a high volume of requests or large amounts of offline labeling needs.
  We present Generative Labeling On Clusters (GLOC) as a solution to provide highly scalable, cost-effective, low latency, and high accuracy online image insight services. GLOC leverages highly optimized image embeddings to form image clusters that are semantically close to each other for the purpose of the type of insights, and summarizes the insights at the cluster level, which effectively generalizes to members in the cluster. At Pinterest, GLOC powers image descriptors and pivot query suggestions for Hybrid Search, which is a multimodal search service enabling users to search with both an image and a text query. Our offline and online A/B tests demonstrate that GLOC significantly outperforms previous methods, delivering improvements in quality and efficiency.
Information Retrieval.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 4th CJ Workshop at KDD 2025 (https://sites.google.com/view/kddcjworkshop2025/accepted-papers), also related: https://arxiv-org.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/2/MOD-93955

Information Retrieval.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
Information Retrieval.summary: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

Information Retrieval.title: Superplatforms are Strategically Compelled to Counteract AI Agents
Information Retrieval.summary: Over the past decades, superplatforms, digital companies that integrate a vast range of third-party services and applications into a single, unified ecosystem, have built their fortunes on monopolizing user attention through targeted advertising and algorithmic content curation. Yet the emergence of AI agents driven by large language models (LLMs) threatens to upend this business model. Agents can not only free user attention with autonomy across diverse platforms and therefore bypass the user-attention-based monetization, but might also become the new entrance for digital traffic. Hence, we argue that superplatforms have to attack AI agents to defend their centralized control of digital traffic entrance. Specifically, we analyze the fundamental conflict between user-attention-based monetization and agent-driven autonomy through the lens of our gatekeeping theory. We show how AI agents can disintermediate superplatforms and potentially become the next dominant gatekeepers, thereby forming the urgent necessity for superplatforms to proactively constrain and attack AI agents. Moreover, we go through the potential technologies for superplatform-initiated attacks, covering a brand-new, unexplored technical area with unique challenges. We have to emphasize that, despite our position, this paper does not advocate for adversarial attacks by superplatforms on AI agents, but rather offers an envisioned trend to highlight the emerging tensions between superplatforms and AI agents. Our aim is to raise awareness and encourage critical discussion for collaborative solutions, prioritizing user interests and perserving the openness of digital ecosystems in the age of AI agents.

Information Retrieval.title: Hidden Distances: How Likert-Scale Spacing Shapes Algorithmic Voting Advice
Information Retrieval.summary: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45\% of VAA users reported following its advice. VAAs typically ask voters and candidates to respond to policy statements on a Likert scale, from ``strongly disagree'' to ``strongly agree'', and recommend candidates whose responses are closest to the voter's. Computing these distances requires assigning numbers to response options, a design choice without an empirical basis, since it is unknown how people perceive the distances between options. Here we show that this seemingly technical choice substantially changes whom voters are matched with. We parameterize the distance between ``(dis)agree'' and ``strongly (dis)agree'' relative to the distance between ``neutral'' and ``(dis)agree'' as $α$, and quantify how it changes recommendations for a popular Danish VAA. We find that moving from equidistant options to doubling this distance can change $37.7\%$ of top candidate matches and $21.9\%$ of top party matches, although no answers change. Low $α$-values favor candidates with strong positions, with some parties receiving up to $ 19.6\%$ more recommendations, while high $α$-values favor moderates. Similarly, female candidates receive fewer recommendations at low $α$ and more at high $α$-values. Our findings demonstrate that undisclosed quantification choices in algorithmic recommenders can carry considerable electoral consequences, and they call for transparency and sensitivity analysis in VAA design. As Likert-based matching also underpins dating platforms and roommate allocation systems, these implications extend well beyond elections.

Information Retrieval.title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

Information Retrieval.title: ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents
Information Retrieval.summary: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive web platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a recommendation-agent framework, termed ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item-page screenshots and uses an OCR tool to produce structured textual evidence for the reasoning backbone. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential update strategy that maintains a bounded textual memory while processing histories longer than the backbone context window; with fixed chunk and memory budgets, the number of update calls grows linearly with history length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To train the dynamic memory updater, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant whose reward combines recommendation-specific information with final-task metrics. Experiments on three Amazon-derived datasets and a controlled post-retrieval protocol show an average relative improvement of 7.58% over the strongest reported baseline across searching, ranking, and judging tasks.

Information Retrieval.title: BRIDGE: Bridging the Semantic Quantization Gap for Generative Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary:
Generative recommendation retrieves items by autoregressively generating Semantic IDs(SIDs), where an RQ-VAE quantizes each item into a hierarchical SID sequence that the decoder generates level by level. We identify an overlooked bottleneck in this paradigm: the Semantic Quantization Gap(SQG). Quantization derives SIDs from rich continuous signals, including codebook centroids, local neighborhood geometry, and level-wise entropy. However, the decoder receives only discrete identifiers and loses the semantic structure that shaped them. This mismatch manifests in three ways: a grounding gap, where the decoder lacks semantic anchors when target-side information is limited; a neighborhood gap, where token-level supervision discards inter-item similarity and exacerbates exposure bias; and a difficulty gap, where computation is allocated uniformly despite generation difficulty diminishing with depth.
  To bridge the SQG, we propose BRIDGE. Codebook-grounded latent reasoning injects frozen quantizer centroids as semantic anchors before SID generation. Privileged EMA self-distillation transfers neighborhood-aware knowledge from a teacher to an on-policy student, preserving inter-item geometry while mitigating exposure bias. Effort-aware recurrence allocates more computation to the challenging early levels and progressively reduces it with depth. Across three Amazon benchmarks, BRIDGE improves Recall@10 and NDCG@10 by 10.9% and 9.7% on average over the strongest baseline (up to 12.6% and 10.7%). In a one-week online A/B experiment on a large-scale e-commerce advertising platform with 5% traffic, BRIDGE improves eCPM by 0.65%.

Information Retrieval.title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

Information Retrieval.title: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation
Information Retrieval.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $α$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.

Information Retrieval.title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Late Chunking encodes an entire document before pooling at chunk boundaries, preserving document context in local retrieval units. Chunk-level post-training improves context-dependent retrieval, but shared context can make semantically similar same-document negatives difficult to distinguish. We study the local decision boundary between a gold chunk and its hardest sibling. Starting from InSeNT, we analyze InSeNT's within-document gradients and show that the entropy of the conditional negative allocation decreases monotonically with the scaling factor at fixed logits. We propose a two-part framework for calibrating document-local chunk boundaries. The first component adapts the discriminative scale from within-document margins, while the second exposes chunk partitions to attention during document encoding. Experiments on ConTEB and NanoBEIR show that the resulting model improves contextual chunk retrieval across the evaluated encoder settings while retaining competitive passage-level retrieval quality; ablations further characterize the distinct roles of adaptive scaling and chunk-aware routing.

Information Retrieval.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
Information Retrieval.summary: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

Information Retrieval.title: CHO-Bench: How Do Context Hints Affect Ad Rankings in LLM Advertising?
Information Retrieval.summary: LLM advertising selects advertisements based on user conversations, where user needs may extend beyond explicit product searches. ChatGPT Ads allows advertisers to provide natural-language context hints describing what they offer, who may find it useful, and when it may be useful, as additional information for ranking advertisements across diverse user conversations. However, how to effectively construct these hints remains unclear. We formulate Context Hint Optimization (CHO) as the problem of constructing context hints to improve an advertisement's ranking under a given budget. Drawing on established marketing frameworks, we develop seven context hint generation strategies covering What, Who, and When, along with a Unified strategy that combines all seven dimensions. We introduce CHO-Bench and conduct over 1.19 million paired evaluations across five datasets using embedding-based and LLM-based rankers. Our results show that context hints improve advertisement rankings under the evaluated offline rankers. While individual strategies achieve similar average gains and Unified offers no consistent advantage, strategy differences become more pronounced under specific generation-ranking configurations, with embedding-based and LLM-based rankers favoring different information dimensions. Increasing the hint budget further improves rankings with diminishing marginal gains. These findings establish an offline benchmark for studying ad-side ranking optimization in LLM advertising and highlight opportunities for model-specific hint selection and budget-aware generation and aggregation.

Information Retrieval.title: Multi-Modal Agricultural Document Understanding at the DAGRI Task
Information Retrieval.summary: Agricultural documents, such as prefectural technical reports and crop calendars, are critical knowledge resources. However, their complex table layouts, significant variations in document length, and dense multi-modal elements pose substantial challenges for automated understanding. To address these issues, the NTCIR-19 DAGRI (Data Analytics for aGRicultural Information) task introduced three subtasks focusing on different dimensions of document intelligence. In the Table Information Extraction (TableIE) task, we developed a multi-stage pipeline combining structure-preserving parsing via MinerU, region-adaptive segmentation for long documents, and a dual-modal (vision-text) extraction strategy for complex work schedules. This approach achieved first place with an exact match score of 0.6566. For Multi-Table Multi-Hop Question Answering (MTMH-QA) over interrelated JSON tables, we adopted an agentic search framework utilizing DCI-Agent to iteratively explore directories via bash commands, reinforced by a cross-model validation mechanism. This yielded a revised accuracy of 0.8444, initially ranked first. In the Figure and Table Question Answering (FiT-QA) task, which requires comprehending single large composite images, we implemented a dual-modal VLM pipeline enhanced by deterministic answer normalization, securing the highest BLEU score. Together, our system effectively addresses regional structural variations, dynamic cross-file evidence discovery, and multi-modal alignment, providing a robust framework for complex agricultural document understanding.

Information Retrieval.title: Proactive Dimension-Adaptive Denoising for Graph Collaborative Filtering via Representation Coherence
Information Retrieval.summary: Implicit feedback in recommender systems contains noisy interactions (e.g., accidental clicks, impulse purchases) that propagate through user-item graphs and contaminate learned representations. Existing explicit denoising methods uniformly rely on training loss to estimate interaction reliability. However, loss is a fundamentally passive signal: it detects noise only after it has caused prediction errors, and it is heavily confounded by training stage, negative sampling, and hard positives. We propose Noise-aware Dimension Learning (NDL), a proactive dimension-adaptive denoising framework. NDL introduces Representation Coherence Detection (RCD), which evaluates the coherence between an interaction representation and the user's historical preference centroid in embedding space, providing an active noise signal independent of loss. RCD and the loss signal are fused via activity-aware weighting (active users rely more on coherence while cold-start users automatically fall back to loss), and the fused estimate drives an interaction-level dimension-adaptive mask that limits the effective representation capacity of unreliable interactions. A lightweight contrastive regularizer further improves embedding uniformity, stabilizing the geometry on which RCD discriminates. On three public benchmarks NDL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art denoising methods, lifting Recall@5 by +17.95% on Amazon-book, +12.33% on Yelp, and +5.63% on MovieLens-1M over the strongest baseline DAR; the core variant without contrastive learning already surpasses DAR on sparser datasets, confirming representation coherence as the primary driver of these gains. NDL is confined to the training loop and is serving-compatible with LightGCN-based production pipelines, adding no online latency or parameters at inference time. Code: https://github.com/GordonDongZHAO/NDL

Information Retrieval.title: A Technique to Model Product Information and User Reviews (MPIUR)
Information Retrieval.summary: Modern e-commerce platforms naturally provide three complementary modalities: textual item descriptions, item images, and user reviews. However, existing multimodal recommendation methods often omit reviews or do not integrate all three modalities within a unified framework. In this paper, we propose MPIUR, a multimodal graph-based recommendation model that encodes reviews in heterogeneous graphs, aligns image and text representations, and adapts collaborative--semantic alignment to item interaction density. Experiments on the Amazon Reviews 2023 Musical Instruments and Baby categories show that MPIUR achieves the best global nDCG@10 and Recall@10 among the evaluated methods on both datasets. It also obtains the best nDCG@10 and Recall@10 on sparse items, indicating that jointly exploiting reviews and multimodal item content is particularly useful when interaction histories are limited.

Information Retrieval.title: Combining Relevant Expert Knowledge Using Mixtures of Feedback Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
Information Retrieval.summary: A neuro-symbolic system should combine only relevant answers from expert agents or other knowledge sources. Using only relevant experts for a given input query becomes ever more important for accuracy and scalability as the knowledge network grows and connects ever more knowledge sources. We extend the standard definition of relevance from the legal theory of evidence: An answer is relevant if and only if it is both probative and material for the matter at hand given the knowledge available. We apply this relevancy scheme to mixing the feedback fuzzy cognitive maps (FCMs) of real or artificial experts. The expert FCM directed causal graphs mix or combine into a common knowledge network. We compare the equilibrium limit-cycle predictions or answers of the experts to the answers of the mixture FCM and then estimate the probative status of answers by their difference or variation. A new Bayes-like theorem de-mixes the knowledge mixture into corresponding posterior-like FCMs that also allow relevancy-based comparisons. The result is a final set of relevancy mixing weights that produces a relevancy-mixed FCM knowledge network for the given query. So different queries produce different relevancy-mixed FCMs. We demonstrate this relevancy approach using generated synthetic FCMs from an actual 13-node expert FCM that models the causes and feedbacks of ischemic-stroke risk.

Information Retrieval.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
Information Retrieval.summary: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
Information Retrieval.comment: Architecture and analysis preprint; no benchmark measurements. Companion research essay and revision notes: https://achiral.ai/research/activation-guided-graph-retrieval

Information Retrieval.title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
Information Retrieval.summary: Banks now train foundation models on ordered sequences of customer events such as transactions, app sessions, and authorizations. Deployed, such a model predicts forward in time, often for customers and merchants absent from training, yet each is evaluated on private data, so no two can be compared. Public benchmarks for such sequences rarely test a period the model has not seen; recommendation studies usually hold out each user's last events instead. We present INTENT (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction), a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training. An audit of 59 public dataset families retains five datasets; the most common defect is the lack of a calendar timestamp that orders events. No date lies within the time span of all five datasets, so each is split at its own cutoff, chosen by one rule fixed before any model is evaluated. Summed over the datasets, every cell holds at least 111,769 users. In reference results the cell determines the best model: a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, a variant that embeds item metadata helps mainly on MicroLens, and repeating the user's last item leads on new items in four of five datasets. This parameter-free control also shows that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff reflects changed behavior rather than the model. The pipeline, the cutoff rule, and the per-cell user counts are publicly available.
Information Retrieval.comment: 4 pages + references and appendix. Accepted at the MFMB workshop at ACM ICAIF '26 (non-archival). Code: https://github.com/kthaisociety/intent

Information Retrieval.title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product
Information Retrieval.summary: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.
Information Retrieval.comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 4-package held-out evaluation; 12,000 evaluated responses

Artificial Intelligence.title: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Bench-MFG: A Benchmark Suite for Learning in Stationary Mean Field Games
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The rise of Mean Field Games (MFGs) has fostered a growing family of algorithms designed to solve large-scale multi-agent systems. However, the field currently lacks a standardized evaluation protocol, forcing researchers to rely on bespoke, isolated, and often simplistic environments. This fragmentation makes it difficult to assess the robustness, generalization, and failure modes of emerging methods. To address this gap, we propose a comprehensive benchmark suite for MFGs, focusing on the discrete-time, discrete-space, stationary setting. We introduce a taxonomy of problem classes, ranging from no-interaction and monotone games to potential and dynamics-coupled games, and provide prototypical environments for each. Furthermore, we present MF-Garnets, a method for generating random MFG instances to facilitate rigorous statistical testing. We benchmark a variety of learning algorithms across these environments, including a novel population-based approach (MF-PSO). To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark for MFGs.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

Artificial Intelligence.title: An offline approach to fNIRS-guided reinforcement learning for robot behavior
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Human-in-the-loop Reinforcement Learning has become a popular approach for training, finetuning, and aligning robot behavior with user preferences. Our paper explores the feasibility of using brain signals via functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to modulate robot learning in simulation. We compare agents trained on passive (observational) versus active (demonstrative) interaction tasks, and test multiple methods for enhancing the RL algorithm with the neural signal, focusing on parameter augmentation in contrast to replacement. We further examine how model granularity and noise affect agent learning. Our results show that this framework is effective. The neural signal improves learning when augmenting trajectory priorities and state-action q-targets. Additionally, the framework learns successfully from offline data, offering a practical alternative for settings where real-time BCI setups are impractical or only limited data is available.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the 4th Workshop on Nonverbal Cues for Human-Robot Cooperative Intelligence (IROS 2026). 5 pages, 3 figures

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Statistical Framework for Algorithmic Collective Action with Multiple Collectives
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As learning systems increasingly shape everyday decisions, Algorithmic Collective Action (ACA), i.e., users coordinating changes to shared data to steer model behavior, offers a complement to regulator-side policy and corporate model design. Real-world collective actions have traditionally been decentralized and fragmented into multiple collectives, despite sharing overarching objectives, with each collective differing in size, strategy, and actionable goals. However, most of the ACA literature focuses on single collective settings. To address this, we propose the first comprehensive statistical framework for ACA with multiple collectives acting on the same system. In particular, we focus on collective action in classification, studying how multiple collectives can influence a classifier's behavior. We provide quantitative statistical bounds on the success of the collectives, considering the role and the interplay of the collectives' sizes and the alignment of their goals. We make such bounds computable by each collective with only partial knowledge of other collectives' sizes and strategies. Finally, we numerically illustrate our framework on simulations inspired by interventions for climate adaptation in smart cities, demonstrating the usefulness of our bounds.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
Artificial Intelligence.summary: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Worse Forces Can Lead to Better Structures: Trajectory-Level Fine-Tuning of Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are commonly trained and evaluated by their ability to reproduce first-principles energies and forces. Practical value, however, is often determined by downstream processes such as structural relaxation. Much of MLIP literature is motivated by the expectation that improving force accuracy will produce correspondingly better downstream behavior. Although this expectation is natural, it may not hold in practice due to model inaccuracies. Here, we demonstrate that force accuracy and relaxation accuracy can be driven in opposite directions. Starting from pretrained MLIPs, we differentiate through relaxation trajectories and optimize the the final structures. This intervention produces increases in force-prediction errors while substantially reducing structural errors. Importantly, this represents a trade-off between two aspects of physical fidelity: the learned forces become less faithful to first-principles forces, while the resulting relaxed structures become more faithful to first-principles predictions. Rather than observing a discrepancy between local quality and downstream performance, we demonstrate that this discrepancy can be induced through optimization. Our findings suggest that MLIPs need not be optimized as approximations of first-principles forces, but can instead learn task-specific vector fields that guide relaxation trajectories toward more accurate final structures. By propagating supervision through complete relaxation trajectories, our framework captures dependencies between successive predictions that are absent when structure--force pairs are treated independently. More broadly, these results demonstrate that conventional force metrics can provide an incomplete assessment of downstream performance and highlights the importance of evaluating scientific machine-learning models within computational workflows.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 10 main pages, total of 18 pages. 5 tables, 10 Figures

Artificial Intelligence.title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Towards Reliable, Generalizable, and Specific In-Context Knowledge Editing via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful but limited by static parametric knowledge that becomes outdated once pretraining ends. Knowledge editing addresses this problem by updating model behavior on target facts without full retraining. In particular, in-context knowledge editing has gained attention because it is training-free and readily applicable to black-box LLMs. Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches improve over fixed retrieval strategies by adapting prompt construction to the quantity-quality trade-off. Despite initial success, they fail to model the prompt as a structured entity under the distinct and often competing objectives of reliability, generality, and specificity. Previous methods largely optimize a single objective and make decisions over only part of the prompt construction process, thereby overlooking both the balance of different objectives and the global organization of demonstrations. We propose Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE), a multi-objective RL algorithm that formulates prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever to optimize competing objectives in knowledge editing, enabling more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction. On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Our work proposes a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes prompt construction for reliable, generalizable, and specific in-context knowledge-editing

Artificial Intelligence.title: Racing to the Starting Line: Measuring Opportunity and Improvement in Cross Country
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Collegiate cross country programs set race schedules without large comparable datasets across courses and conditions. Using the comprehensive-era National Running Club Database (NRCD; 23,360 results; 7,056 athletes; 2023-2025), where course and weather coverage exceed 99%, we ask what public results can identify about seasonal improvement, measurement, and racing opportunity. Hierarchical models of Standardized times recover pooled within-season improvement of about -5.7 s/week for men and -5.2 for women, but reading those slopes as fitness requires residual meet difficulty not to track the calendar: crossed meet effects can erase the week slope, while repeating-venue effects recover a clearer men's estimate under a weaker assumption. After the opener, race-1-only forecasts of who will improve are near noise (held-out R^2 ~ 0). Weather standardization remains a useful convention (Converted Only overstates first-to-last gains by about 15-21 s relative to Standardized), and prospectively trained venue factors modestly help where prior course data exist. Successful programs race more and place higher at nationals, but that may not be why they win: the schedule-placement link is between programs and is entangled with roster size, not evidence that changing one team's race count raises nationals place.

Artificial Intelligence.title: LUCQUE: A lung cancer screening dataset from Québec for reliable AI evaluation
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
BACKGROUND: AI-based tools are expected to play a key role in lung cancer screening (LCS). The evaluation of these tools often relied on private datasets or fragmented public datasets with inconsistent availability of clinical data and expert nodule annotations. This has hindered reproducibility, comparability, and independent assessment of AI tools. To address these gaps, we present LUCQUE, a novel, large, comprehensively annotated dataset derived from LDCT lung cancer screening in Québec, which is accessible for reliable AI evaluation.
  METHODS: LUCQUE was curated and is hosted on PARADIM, a digital infrastructure supporting DICOM data de-identification, annotation, long-term storage and analysis. LDCT scans and clinical information were combined to a curated collection and complemented by voxel-level, expert-derived pulmonary nodule and cyst segmentations, and Lung-RADS-based lesion characteristics. Key dataset characteristics and statistics were reported, including participant demographics, imaging parameters, radiological findings, and segmented lesion characteristics. Dataset analyses were conducted according to PARADIM's model-to-data approach, in which user code is executed on the platform such that data remains on premise.
  RESULTS: LUCQUE currently comprises 1,678 LDCT baseline studies from 1,678 participants. Most studies were classified as Lung-RADS 2. A total of 1,776 pulmonary nodules and 60 cysts were annotated, with a median (interquartile range) volume of $89\,(56,\,159)\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ and $1,384\,(589,\,3793)\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ respectively.
